Installing a sediment filter near the pressure tank is also recommended to help protect the home’s plumbing system from debris coming from the well.

Well water commonly carries sand, silt, and other sediment that can enter the home’s plumbing system. By installing a sediment filter immediately after the pressure tank, the filter will capture these particles before the water continues through the rest of the home.

Benefits of installing a sediment filter include:
	•	Removing sand, silt, and debris coming from the well
	•	Protecting plumbing fixtures such as faucets, toilets, and shower valves from sediment buildup
	•	Preventing premature wear on appliances such as the water heater, washing machine, and treatment equipment
	•	Helping protect the Sanitizer Plus system by reducing the amount of sediment entering the unit

The sediment filter would be installed on the main water line near the pressure tank, allowing it to filter the water before it enters the home’s plumbing system and before it reaches the water treatment equipment.

This addition will help maintain cleaner water throughout the home and extend the life of plumbing fixtures and water treatment equipment.

Installing a UV light system near the pressure tank is also recommended to help protect the home’s drinking water from harmful bacteria that can sometimes be present in well water.

Private well systems are not treated by municipal facilities, so bacteria such as E. coli and other microorganisms can potentially enter the water supply. A UV disinfection system uses ultraviolet light to neutralize bacteria and other microorganisms as the water passes through the unit.

Benefits of installing a UV light system include:
	•	Eliminating harmful bacteria and microorganisms that may be present in well water
	•	Providing safe drinking water throughout the home
	•	Continuous disinfection without adding chemicals to the water
	•	Protecting the household’s health by ensuring the water supply remains sanitary

The UV light system would be installed on the main water line near the pressure tank, allowing the water to be disinfected before it enters the home’s plumbing system. This placement ensures that all water distributed throughout the home has been properly treated.

Adding a UV system, along with the sediment filter and Sanitizer Plus treatment system, will create a more complete well-water treatment setup that improves water quality, protects plumbing fixtures, and ensures a safe and healthy water supply for the home.

The existing Waterfall water softener is old and no longer operational. The home’s water supply is provided by a private well. Testing shows the water hardness is approximately 22 grains per gallon, which is considered very hard water. In addition, the water is highly acidic with a pH of 5.5, making it corrosive to plumbing components and fixtures over time. Acidic water can deteriorate copper piping, valves, fixtures, and appliances connected to the water system.

Due to the combination of high hardness, low pH (acidic water), and the potential presence of iron commonly found in well water, the technician highly recommends replacing the existing system with a Sanitizer Plus treatment system. This system is designed to treat multiple well-water issues simultaneously by:
	•	Softening the water to reduce hardness buildup in plumbing and fixtures
	•	Neutralizing acidic water to help prevent corrosion of piping and equipment
	•	Removing iron and other common well-water contaminants

The proposed Sanitizer Plus system would be installed near the water heater for optimal access to the home’s main water distribution.

Installation details are as follows:
	•	The inlet to the Sanitizer Plus will be connected to the main cold water supply line before the washing machine connection to ensure treated water is distributed throughout the home.
	•	The backwash drain line will be connected to the main drain line located above the installation area.
	•	A dedicated electrical outlet is already available near the installation location to power the system.

This installation will significantly improve overall water quality while protecting the home’s plumbing system from the damaging effects of hard and acidic well water.

The existing concrete double-compartment utility sink currently drains directly onto the basement floor and relies on the sump pump pit to remove the wastewater. In addition, the washing machine also discharges directly into the sump pump pit. This setup is not ideal and does not meet proper plumbing practices for handling greywater discharge.

The technician will remove the existing double-compartment concrete utility sink and replace it with a new utility sink and faucet. The new utility sink will be properly connected to a laundry pump system to ensure wastewater is discharged correctly.

Installation and modifications will include the following:
	•	The new utility sink drain will connect directly to the new laundry pump basin.
	•	The laundry pump discharge line will be piped to the main drain located above the installation area to properly remove wastewater from the pump basin.
	•	The laundry pump vent will be installed and terminated to the exterior through the side of the home above the washing machine to allow proper venting of the system.
	•	The technician will repipe a section of the main drain line to allow the laundry pump discharge to connect properly and to ensure the installation complies with International Plumbing Code (IPC) standards.
	•	Once installed, the washing machine will discharge into the new utility sink, which will then drain into the laundry pump basin.

An electrical outlet is already available near the installation area to power the laundry pump system.

This installation will provide a proper and code-compliant method of removing wastewater from the basement laundry area, preventing greywater from entering the sump system and improving the overall function and reliability of the drainage system.

Technician found a puddle of water on the garage floor near the chimney, approximately 3–4 feet away from the garage hose bib. Technician determined there are no other plumbing fixtures or water lines near the chimney, other than the plumbing located in the basement along the wall adjacent to the garage.

Technician inspected the basement plumbing and identified the water heater, hot and cold water supply lines, and the cold water line supplying the garage hose bib. All plumbing lines were inspected, and no leaks were found. Of the plumbing fixtures and water lines in this area, the garage hose bib was the only potential source that could account for the water accumulating near the chimney.

Technician cleaned up the existing puddle and turned on the garage hose bib to observe how the water traveled across the garage floor. Technician also recorded a video of the water flow. The water followed the path of least resistance toward the chimney and away from the garage door, consistent with the location of the puddle.

Based on these findings, technician believes the puddle may have been caused by the garage hose bib being left on, allowing water to travel across the garage floor and collect near the chimney. During the inspection, technician also noticed the hose bib has a slow drip, indicating a possible failure of the packing nut. This ongoing drip could also contribute to water accumulating in the same area.

Recommendation: Technician recommends replacing the existing garage hose bib to correct the slow drip and help prevent further water accumulation on the garage floor.

i.439618474:
Today, LPH was called out due to an issue with the lamppost circuit tripping the breaker.

Upon evaluation, I removed the switch to verify that it was not the cause of the issue. The breaker continued to trip. I then disconnected both the light fixture and GFCI, but the breaker continued to trip. This indicated that the issue was likely within the wiring.

After speaking with Mike, I was informed that there had been a previous splice in the mulch bed. We excavated the area, located the existing splice, and cut the wire at that location. After doing so, the breaker stopped tripping. I then installed a new splice, and the breaker held without tripping.

I informed Mike that, due to the deteriorated condition of the existing wiring, I strongly recommend replacing the entire wire run and PVC conduit to provide a reliable, long-term solution.

We also discussed the possibility of installing two additional Cadet switches: one to control the lamppost and another to control the front exterior light.

Mike advised that, for the time being, his preference is to have the existing wiring spliced and repaired rather than proceed with a complete replacement

Upon installing the splice kit we found there is a direct short which we didn’t see since we didn’t hook up ground to test. That section of wire wil need to be replaced. I provided several option to see what fits there needs. Emailed invoice.

i.439781034:
LPH returned to the home to complete the previously discussed installation of a premium whole-home surge protection device at the main electrical panel. This device is designed to protect the home’s electrical system and connected equipment from damaging voltage spikes and transient surges before they can travel throughout the home’s wiring.

Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but the majority of power surges actually originate inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and even garage door openers create small electrical surges, known as microsurges, every time their motors cycle on and off. While each individual surge is small, thousands of these microsurges occur over time and gradually wear down the sensitive electronic components found in today’s modern appliances and equipment.

Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these surges away from the home’s electrical system, reducing cumulative damage to expensive electronics and appliances. This is especially important in newer homes, where nearly every major appliance contains sophisticated circuit boards and microprocessors that are more sensitive to voltage fluctuations than older equipment.

In addition to internally generated microsurges, whole-home surge protection provides a critical first line of defense against larger surges originating from the utility company, electrical grid switching events, nearby lightning strikes, or power being restored after an outage.

Benefits of Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection Include:

* Protects HVAC systems, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
* Helps safeguard televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart home devices.
* Reduces the long-term effects of everyday microsurges that gradually degrade electronic components.
* Helps extend the service life of modern appliances by reducing electrical stress on internal circuit boards.
* Helps minimize the likelihood of costly repairs or premature equipment replacement due to surge damage.
* Provides continuous protection for the home’s electrical system without relying solely on individual plug-in surge strips.
* Offers added peace of mind during storms, utility switching events, and unexpected power outages.

Premium Surge Protection Warranty & Replacement Coverage

The installed surge protection device also provides additional protection beyond the device itself. If the surge protector is ever sacrificed or fails as a result of a covered surge event, it is backed by a lifetime warranty and coverage of up to $100,000 toward covered damage to the home’s electrical components and connected equipment, subject to the manufacturer’s warranty terms and conditions.

If the surge protector ever needs to be replaced under warranty, the replacement device is provided at no charge. LPH will also handle the replacement installation for a $150 labor charge, helping make future warranty replacement straightforward and affordable.

This means the homeowner is not simply purchasing a surge protector; they are adding a long-term layer of protection to the home’s electrical system while also having manufacturer-backed coverage in the event of a significant surge.

Completed Installation

LPH returned to the home and successfully installed the premium whole-home surge protection device at the main electrical panel. Installation was completed, tested, and verified to be operating properly, providing the home with an additional layer of protection against both internally generated electrical surges and external power disturbances.

Today’s invoice will be emailed to the homeowner. Thank you for choosing LPH and allowing us the opportunity to complete this upgrade for your home!

i.439792763:
Arrived tonight to address furnace short cycling on a gas furnace. Customer stated this had gone on for longer than a week and that the systems were approximately 3 years old. I found that furnace would ignite gas then shut down a few seconds later, indicating a flame sensing issue. Due to the late hour, customer requested we forego the full system evaluation. However, I did test combustion on the furnace after cleaning the flame sensor and it stayed lit. Also inspected heat exchanger and checked temperatures.

Upon arrival I noted the large amounts of white powder inside the furnace and along many of the joints in the venting, which indicates exhaust gases are condensing inside the flue, possibly due to backdrafting. Plastic rings on top of the water heater were partially melted. While we would need to spend more time examining the venting system to ensure it is constructed properly, other findings suggest the mechanical room could be going into negative pressure causing backdraft. Filter racks are missing their slide in covers and have been, per the customer, for many years. This allows air to be pulled from the room into the furnaces when they run. The room itself may also not be providing enough combustion air. To prevent this damaging and potentially dangerous occurrence, I recommend sealing the filter doors and leaving the door to the mechanical room open until we return on the 30th for a heating system check. We will inspect further at that time 

Furnace is now heating.

i.439878352: We were called out to evaluate the overhead lighting issue that the homeowners were dealing with. Upon arrival, we were informed that the dimmer switch for the dining room light would not work at all. The homeowners also stated that they flipped the breaker inside the electrical panel, which did not seem to solve the issue. We started our thorough evaluation at the main electrical panel to assess the voltages coming into the house and wiring connections before working our way to the dimmer switch. Upon opening up the panel, we immediately identified presence of corrosion on the main neutral bar and rust at the bottom of the panel. This leads to the conclusion that water was getting into this panel by somehow, so we went to investigate where the water was coming from. We were able to identify that the outside service wire from the meter base to the panel was completely cracked open and in really bad shape. We highly recommend that the entire service system be replaced with the new meter base, the addition of an emergency disconnect, and a brand new 200 amp interior panel. We also provided an option to replace the immediate components affected by this open wire. The homeowners wanted an option to just replace the wire that’s in really bad shape and reevaluate the remaining components at a date, which is something we definitely can take care of. We did confirm the dimmer switch for the dining room to be the failed component of the system after all of the test that we conducted at this unit. The corrosion inside the panel definitely can play a factor in the system failure along with other components in the home in the future. However, at this time we confirmed that the age of the dimmer switch was the main reason of the failure. Once we figured out the main issue, we provided accurate options to remedy all of our concerns as well as the homeowners primary concern. The basic electrical package was approved by the homeowner and partially completed today. This option included replacing the outside service wire only and replacing the dimmer switch in the dining room. We replaced the dimmer switch today but will return to replace the wire. Since we are only replacing the wire and not the electrical panel, which is recommended by us, we cannot warranty or own any responsibility for this electrical panel or meter base. Remaining options and invoice will be emailed to the homeowners. We thank you for trusting LPH and we look forward to servicing you in the future.

i.440263941: This morning I arrived at the Roman family home to conduct their annual electrical system and safety check. Upon performing a thorough evaluation of the homes main electrical service I found only one primary discrepancy which is in relation to the dryer circuit. I noted that the dryer is situated under a 30A 240v system (30A breaker, 30A appliance, 30A rated 240v dryer plug.) however, the wire for this circuit is 12-2, while this wiring can be used for 240v circuits, it is only safe and allowable for a maximum of 20A, as opposed to the 30A system it is being used on. This undersized wire, paired with an oversized breaker can lead to overheating of the wiring, and potentially a failure to trip situation if the wire becomes any more overloaded than it currently is. I have provided an estimate to upsize this circuit to its appropriate 10AWG wiring counterpart. A secondary estimate was provided regarding the homes main power supply wiring on the outside of the home. I noted that while the main SEU service wiring had been replaced at some point, the bottom section of wiring that comes out of the external meterbase and feeds the breaker panel was left original. If you review the photos I have attached you will see the difference in condition of the top half wiring, as opposed to the section on the bottom that enters into the home. The estimate I have provided covered replacing the approximately 5’ section of wiring that feeds the breaker panel. Otherwise the home appears to be in good overall condition electrically. If you have any questions, or if you would like to move forward with either of these options, please do not hesitate to contact us. Thanks you for your time and take care!

e.440464771: LPH will replace non-code compliant undersized dryer circuit. Currently the circuit is a 12-2 wire rated for a maximum of 20A, on a 30A breaker with a 30A appliance. LPH will upsize circuit to 10AWG accordingly.

i.440264193:
Performed heating system checks on 3 gas furnaces and the steam boilers. Please see attached evaluation forms for measurements and photos. At this time the 3 furnaces are all running within specifications with no further recommended maintenance. There re some concerns on the steam boilers, much of them being a recap from last winters visit:

1. The secondary boiler does not have its own, independent low water cutoff. Due to the age of the system and current conditions inside the boilers, this poses a hazard that sludge could prevent the boiler from filling and it could dry fire, and hazardous condition.
2. There is significant rust and sludge buildup inside the boilers, especially the secondary. Sight glass turned brown right after firing. 
3. The canopy that sits on top of the heat exchangers on both boilers is no longer sealed, meaning we can now look into the fire side of the boiler from the outside. This poses a hazard of combustion gases escaping. 
4. General maintenance, the boilers should be serviced yearly to prevent clogging of safety devices 

******Given their condition, I recommended not running the boilers until these issues are addressed.****** 

I am sending over an option to clean the boilers, flush and treat them for sludge buildup, install a low water cutoff on the secondary boiler, and install a spill switch on the exhaust flue. 

We discussed the above issues, as well as the upcoming renovations and the need to temporarily uninstall the radiator in the master bathroom. I am sending over an option for uninstalling and reinstalling that radiator if the renovating contractor is unable to do so. 

I well send the following information as a follow up email:

We went over filter change schedules and how to change the Aprilaire media. Attic unit filter is quite clean still. Kitchen unit has more dust accumulation but should still be ok until march at the earliest. 

Replacement media:
Attic Unit: Aprilaire 513
Crawlspace Unit: Aprilaire 113

Both should be replaced every 6 to 12 months. Attic unit so far is on track to be good for 12 months but please monitor and change as needed. Quarterly checks would suffice.

i.440298696:
LPH arrived at the home to perform a complete electrical system check evaluation. During our inspection, we reviewed the electrical panel, breakers, grounding and bonding, safety devices, receptacles, switches, and other accessible electrical components throughout the home.

During today’s evaluation, we discussed the following findings and recommendations with the homeowner:

1. Outdoor Receptacle Replacement & Weather Protection

LPH recommends replacing the existing rusted and deteriorated outdoor receptacles with new weather-resistant (WR) receptacles and extra-duty in-use bubble covers.

The rear outdoor receptacle, which is frequently used, currently does not have GFCI protection. This is an important safety concern because outdoor receptacles are exposed to moisture and changing weather conditions. GFCI protection helps reduce the risk of electrical shock by monitoring the flow of electricity and shutting off power when an electrical imbalance is detected.

The front outdoor receptacle is currently GFCI protected; however, years of exposure and deterioration have compromised its condition, causing repeated tripping of the interior GFCI. Replacing the deteriorated receptacle will help address the nuisance tripping and restore dependable outdoor protection.

The new weather-resistant receptacles and extra-duty bubble covers will provide additional protection against rain, moisture, and environmental exposure, including when cords are plugged in.

2. Whole-Home Surge Protection Installation

LPH also recommends installing whole-home surge protection to provide an additional layer of protection for the home’s electrical system and connected equipment.

Electrical surges can enter the home from outside sources, such as lightning activity, utility company switching, transformer issues, and fluctuations on the incoming electrical service. These events can introduce sudden increases in voltage that travel through the home’s wiring and potentially damage sensitive electronics and appliances.

Surges can also originate from inside the home. Everyday appliances and equipment, including air conditioners, heat pumps, refrigerators, furnaces, washing machines, dryers, dishwashers, microwaves, and other motor-driven equipment, can create smaller electrical surges when their motors or compressors start and stop.

Although these smaller fluctuations may not immediately damage equipment, repeated exposure can gradually contribute to deterioration of sensitive electronic components.

Installing a whole-home surge protector at the electrical panel helps defend against both incoming surges from outside the home and internally generated voltage spikes. It works by monitoring electrical voltage and redirecting excess voltage away from the home’s electrical circuits when a surge occurs.

This added protection is especially valuable for today’s appliances, televisions, computers, HVAC equipment, and other electronics that rely on sensitive circuit boards and electronic controls. While no surge protector can prevent every possible electrical event or guarantee that equipment will never be damaged, whole-home protection is an excellent investment in helping reduce the risk of costly electrical damage.

Homeowner Discussion & Next Steps

LPH reviewed both recommendations and available options with the homeowner during today’s visit. The homeowner expressed interest in moving forward with taking care of these items soon.

In the meantime, LPH will send the estimates along with today’s electrical system check evaluation via email so the homeowner can review everything and plan accordingly.

Thank you for taking the time to walk through the home and discuss the electrical system with us. We appreciate the opportunity to help maintain the safety and reliability of your home’s electrical system. Please take your time reviewing the recommendations, and we look forward to helping you get these items taken care of soon. Thank you for choosing LPH!

LPH recommends replacing the existing rusted and deteriorated outdoor receptacles with new weather-resistant (WR) receptacles and extra-duty in-use bubble covers. The current rear outdoor receptacle, which is frequently used, does not have GFCI protection, leaving it without the proper protection against electrical shock in outdoor conditions.

The front outdoor receptacle is currently GFCI protected; however, years of exposure and deterioration have compromised its condition, resulting in repeated nuisance tripping of the interior GFCI.

Replacing both receptacles will restore proper outdoor protection, provide dependable GFCI safety, and help prevent moisture-related deterioration. The new extra-duty bubble covers will also provide added protection while allowing cords to remain plugged in with the cover securely closed.

Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection
LPH will install a premium whole-home surge protection device at the home’s main electrical panel. This device is designed to protect the home’s electrical system and connected equipment from damaging voltage spikes and transient surges before they can travel throughout the home’s wiring.
Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but the majority of power surges actually originate inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and even garage door openers create small electrical surges—known as microsurges—every time their motors cycle on and off. While each individual surge is small, thousands of these microsurges occur over time and gradually wear down the sensitive electronic components found in today’s modern appliances and equipment.
Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these surges away from the home’s electrical system, reducing cumulative damage to expensive electronics and appliances. This is especially important in newer homes, where nearly every major appliance contains sophisticated circuit boards and microprocessors that are far more sensitive to voltage fluctuations than older equipment.
In addition to protecting against internally generated microsurges, whole-home surge protection also provides a critical first line of defense against larger surges originating from the utility company, switching events on the electrical grid, nearby lightning strikes, or power being restored after an outage.
Benefits of premium whole-home surge protection include:
	• Protects HVAC systems, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
	• Helps safeguard sensitive electronics such as televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart home devices.
	• Reduces the long-term effects of everyday microsurges that slowly degrade electronic components.
	• Can help extend the service life of modern appliances and equipment by reducing electrical stress on internal circuit boards.
	• Helps minimize the likelihood of costly repairs or premature equipment replacement due to surge damage.
	• Provides continuous protection for the entire home’s electrical system without relying solely on individual plug-in surge strips.
	• Offers added peace of mind during storms, utility switching events, and unexpected power outages.
As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

Premium Surge Protection Warranty & Replacement Coverage

The installed surge protection device also provides additional protection beyond the device itself. If the surge protector is ever sacrificed or fails as a result of a covered surge event, the device is backed by a lifetime warranty and coverage of up to $100,000 toward covered damage to the home’s electrical components and connected equipment, subject to the manufacturer’s warranty terms and conditions.

If the surge protector ever needs to be replaced under the warranty, the replacement device is provided at no charge. LPH will also handle the replacement installation for a $150 labor charge, helping make future warranty replacement straightforward and affordable for the homeowner.

This means the homeowner is not simply purchasing a surge protector—they are adding a long-term layer of protection to the home’s electrical system while also having manufacturer-backed coverage in the event of a significant surge.

As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

Out to home today for the yearly plumbing system check. Upon arrival to home, there were two concerns. First item has to do with the dishwasher. Homeowner is planning to replace their dishwasher and wanted to verify if there would be any issues during replacement. The other concern has to do with a leak from the bath tub. Homeowner states anytime they use the tub, they notice water in the basement. Upon evaluation, found water to leak down into the wall when water is splashed on the handle. Also identified corrosion at the waste and overflow. Corrosion at the tub shoe could be caused from runoff water from the leak above as the connections appear to be newer. Provided all solutions for leak from tub. 

From there, performed full home plumbing inspection. Tested water quality and found water to be extremely hard. Talked about corrective measures to improve water quality inside the home. At this time, homeowner is not interested in a water softener system. UV system is 29 days away from being due for service. Homeowner states they take care of the UV service. Suggested possibly using a more standard 20 micron filter to get longer life out of the filters before changing. Also talked about installation of a backwashing sediment and turbidity filter to eliminate need to change filters. Inspected and performed routine flush on 3 year old water heater system. Lastly, checked over well system and ensured safe pressure thresholds inside the home. 

Went over all recommendations based on inspection performed today. Homeowner approved replacement of the dishwasher shut off valve. Homeowner is aware that after the repair, the dishwasher will be disconnected from the water supply ready for the new appliance to be installed. Shut down water to home and removed old valve from cabinet. Installed new quarter turn shut off valve with standardized connections. Restored water to home and verified no leaks were present. Repair performed today is guaranteed for one year. Other pricing provided today is valid for 60 days. Thank you for trusting LPH.

Technician reviewed available repair and improvement options to help maintain proper system performance and prevent future plumbing problems.

Homeowner did not want the 2nd floor master bathroom inspected at this time.

2nd Floor Hallway Bathroom – Plumbing Recommendations
- Toilet: Technician found that the toilet fill valve is not functioning properly and is not consistently filling the toilet tank. Technician recommends replacing the existing fill valve and flapper to restore proper toilet operation.
- Lavatory Drain: The lavatory drain is not draining properly. Technician recommends cleaning the pop-up assembly and P-trap to remove accumulated soap scum and hair that may be restricting drainage. If testing determines that the blockage is further down the drain line, additional charges would apply.
- Tub/Shower: Technician found that the tub spout diverter is not functioning properly and is not diverting water to the showerhead. Technician recommends replacing the existing tub spout with a new tub spout equipped with a diverter.

Main Floor Powder Room Toilet: Technician found that the toilet flapper is worn and not sealing properly. Technician recommends replacing the existing flapper to restore a proper seal and prevent water from continuously leaking from the tank into the bowl.

Main Floor Kitchen Sink: Technician found that the left-side basket strainer on the double-bowl kitchen sink is rusted and corroded. Technician recommends replacing the existing basket strainer to restore proper drainage and help prevent potential leaks.

Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 7 grains per gallon (GPG) and the chlorine level to be 1.0 ppm. A hardness level of 7 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, showerheads, and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a City Soft water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the City Soft system is near the existing water heater. The cold water inlet would come from near the water meter approximately 30’ away, as well as the outlet of the water softener. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing copper main drain approximately 30’ away.The system also requires a dedicated electrical outlet for operation and regeneration cycles. The home’s electrical panel is located approximately 15 feet away, and an outlet will need to be installed and provided at the equipment location prior to or as part of the installation. Once installed, the system will provide conditioned water to the entire home and help minimize the long-term effects of hard water and chlorine exposure on the plumbing system.

We test for drinkability by measuring the level of total dissolved solids(TDS) measured in parts per million. At the kitchen sink and shower, the TDS was between 345ppm and 350ppm. When we tested the water at the faucet Cara uses, we tested it at 519ppm. The pH at all three faucets was the same. What could be happening is the break down of a PEX fitting or early degradation of the faucet itself. We really weren’t able to give an exact answer to what the problem is at this point. An estimate has been provided for whole house water filtration.

If you have any other questions or concerns that arise after today’s visit, please do not hesitate to give us a call. Thank you for continuing to trust Lancaster Plumbing and Heating with all of your home service needs. 
This estimate includes Lancaster Plumbing and Heating’s dispatch fee.

i.440463746: Upon arrival the technician located the sewer main to the left of the driveway.  The technician then used a sewer camera to inspect the sewer main in both directions, to the house and to the street.  The found 2 small dents in the top of the piping going to the house and nothing going to the street. The technician did find that the whole house trap is cast iron and appears to be holding sludge in the line. Any cast iron piping underground has a life expectancy of approximately 30-40 years before it starts go bad. Replacing the cast iron trap with PVC would allow for better flow through the trap and less sludge build up. The technician will provided a solution to replace the trap with a new PVC trap.

The homes life safety devices consisting of smoke/ carbon monoxide detectors as well as GFCI receptacles, were up to code and in working order. All outlets and switches were properly functioning with no signs of wiring or device failures. LPH was called out due to an issue with several lights not functioning properly. Upon performing my troubleshooting and evaluation, I discovered a faulty breaker in the subpanel that was contributing to the issue.

During my inspection, I also noticed that both electrical panels are approximately 40 years old, which exceeds the typical recommended service life of 30–35 years. I explained to the homeowner that aging electrical panels can increase the risk of electrical hazards, unexpected failures, and power outages. I also explained that when one breaker begins to fail, it can be an indication of age-related deterioration, and other breakers may experience similar issues down the road.

Additionally, I found that all devices were improperly terminated using the backstab connection method. When I removed one of the devices, the wire came out with very little effort, demonstrating the potential for loose connections and unreliable electrical performance.

I presented a premium option that included replacing both the main electrical panel and subpanel, along with replacing all backstabbed devices. I also provided two additional options for consideration.

I reviewed all my findings with Kevin’s wife and then contacted Kevin directly to discuss the inspection results and available options. Kevin elected to proceed with the immediate repair option. Payment was collected over the phone. After payment was processed, Kevin mentioned that they had a $50 coupon. I informed him that I would contact the office to have the $50 reimbursement addressed.

Today, I replaced the faulty 15-amp breaker and the three-way switch. All work was completed successfully, and the system was tested to verify proper operation.

Thank you for trusting LPH with your electrical needs. I appreciate the opportunity to assist you and look forward to working with you again in the future.

Dispatch for no heat on ~6 year old gas furnace. System was locked out on an igniter relay error code. Igniter was notably oxidized, but the board was not energizing it. I inspected the system and found severe rusting on the internal and external sides of the heat exchanger. Also found pieces from several filters inside the blower housing and cabinet. The existing filter rack is incorrect for this setup and improperly installed. Furnace is resting on the furnace rack with little support on the outside edges. Given my findings, we discussed replacing the control board and hot surface igniter, replacing the heat exchanger, and cleaning the furnace. We also discussed whether to fix the furnace then test the heat exchanger or do it all in one shot. I also recommended installing a new filter system on the return side so we can abandon the existing filter rack.

Replaced control board, HSI, and Heat Exchanger. Cleaned Furnace

Customer also signed up for SPP membership. 

During my repairs I found the water heater expansion tank is actively leaking after having rusted through the body. There is significant rusting and water damage to the water heater. I am sending over an option to replace the water heater or to replace just the expansion tank, but would highly recommend replacing the entire water heater. We can also come out for the annual SPP Plumbing Evaluation if there are any other plumbing concerns in the home or you are interested in a tankless water heater. 

Once repairs were completed, I performed the annual heating system check. Furnace is now clean and operating, but it is running hot due to reduced airflow. i.440789621:
Today I was dispatched to investigate the hot tub tripping the GFCI breaker.

Upon inspection, I found that the GFCI breaker was tripping approximately every 3–4 minutes. I also found that if the breaker was reset and the heater was manually activated, the breaker would trip immediately.

After further research, I determined that the hot tub runs through a 3–4 minute regeneration cycle to verify proper water flow before activating the heating element. This timing correlates with when the breaker was tripping, indicating that the issue is likely related to the heating element or another internal component of the hot tub.

The existing GFCI breaker is also older. GFCI breakers can become more prone to nuisance tripping as they age. Although I do not believe replacing the breaker will resolve the underlying issue, I recommend replacing it to ensure proper and reliable operation once the hot tub repairs have been completed.

The invoice and estimate for the spa disconnect box have been emailed.

We also provided an option to just replace the meter base which was the main concern for Tom. LPH arrived to begin the annual electrical system check. Upon arrival, no electrical concerns/questions were reported prior to our electrical inspection. 

We began our evaluation at the main electrical/distribution panel. This is where we assessed the internal conditions, age, connections and voltage readings. During this inspection, all of the inspected parameters meet the required threshold for a healthy panel. 

We discovered that there’s no system put in place to protect appliances/electronics from spikes of electric which target the sensitive components inside these units. A whole home surge protection device is recommended if the homeowners were interested in  protecting their main utility equipment with a one time investment unit.

Next, we inspected all of the protective systems for personnel and equipment in the home such as the smoke detectors, GFI protection devices, and the grounding system. First, we discovered that the water meter does not meet today’s grounding standards to protect against any leakage of electricity from traveling on the pipes. The next was confirmation that all of the existing smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors are up-to-date. However, we identified that the basement and first floor do not have any CO detectors and the bedrooms don’t have any smoke detectors. The homeowner informed us that the bedrooms doors always stay open unless someone is briefly occupying it. Lastly, we identified two areas with missing GFI protection, which is the exterior outlets and for the washer in the basement. All other devices in the home were tested and functioning properly prior to leaving today.

We provided options to remedy all of our electrical recommendations, which was presented today. All of the options that were not approved will be emailed along with the electrical evaluation form and invoice for today’s visit. We thank you for allowing us in your home to service you and we look forward to servicing you in the future.

During the electrical system evaluation, LPH identified several additional opportunities to improve electrical safety, protection, and functionality throughout the home. The following options were reviewed with the homeowner:

1. Exterior Receptacle Replacement

LPH recommends replacing two existing exterior receptacles that are showing signs of corrosion. Both will be replaced with new weather-resistant receptacles designed to better withstand outdoor moisture and environmental exposure. This will help reduce the risk of moisture-related deterioration, unreliable connections, and premature device failure.

2. Washing Machine GFCI Protection

LPH will install a new GFCI-protected receptacle for the washing machine in the mechanical room. GFCI protection is designed to help protect against electrical shock by shutting off power when a ground fault is detected. This is especially important around laundry equipment and areas where moisture may be present.

3. Whole-Home Surge Protection

Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection
LPH will install a premium whole-home surge protection device at the home’s main electrical panel. This device is designed to protect the home’s electrical system and connected equipment from damaging voltage spikes and transient surges before they can travel throughout the home’s wiring.
Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but the majority of power surges actually originate inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and even garage door openers create small electrical surges—known as microsurges—every time their motors cycle on and off. While each individual surge is small, thousands of these microsurges occur over time and gradually wear down the sensitive electronic components found in today’s modern appliances and equipment.
Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these surges away from the home’s electrical system, reducing cumulative damage to expensive electronics and appliances. This is especially important in newer homes, where nearly every major appliance contains sophisticated circuit boards and microprocessors that are far more sensitive to voltage fluctuations than older equipment.
In addition to protecting against internally generated microsurges, whole-home surge protection also provides a critical first line of defense against larger surges originating from the utility company, switching events on the electrical grid, nearby lightning strikes, or power being restored after an outage.
Benefits of premium whole-home surge protection include:
	• Protects HVAC systems, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
	• Helps safeguard sensitive electronics such as televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart home devices.
	• Reduces the long-term effects of everyday microsurges that slowly degrade electronic components.
	• Can help extend the service life of modern appliances and equipment by reducing electrical stress on internal circuit boards.
	• Helps minimize the likelihood of costly repairs or premature equipment replacement due to surge damage.
	• Provides continuous protection for the entire home’s electrical system without relying solely on individual plug-in surge strips.
	• Offers added peace of mind during storms, utility switching events, and unexpected power outages.
As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

Premium Surge Protection Warranty & Replacement Coverage

The installed surge protection device also provides additional protection beyond the device itself. If the surge protector is ever sacrificed or fails as a result of a covered surge event, the device is backed by a lifetime warranty and coverage of up to $100,000 toward covered damage to the home’s electrical components and connected equipment, subject to the manufacturer’s warranty terms and conditions.

If the surge protector ever needs to be replaced under the warranty, the replacement device is provided at no charge. LPH will also handle the replacement installation for a $150 labor charge, helping make future warranty replacement straightforward and affordable for the homeowner.

This means the homeowner is not simply purchasing a surge protector—they are adding a long-term layer of protection to the home’s electrical system while also having manufacturer-backed coverage in the event of a significant surge.

As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

4. Customer-Supplied Ceiling Fan Replacement

LPH will remove the existing ceiling fan and install the new customer-supplied ceiling fan with integrated light. All necessary electrical connections will be made, and the new fan and light will be tested for proper operation.

Based on the inspection and test results, LPH determined that the heat exchanger is cracked and that the furnace is unsafe to operate at this time.

LPH strongly recommends keeping the furnace shut down and scheduling an appointment with our Comfort Consultant to review replacement options.

i.441734727:
Reevaluate the sewer solution 
During the original visit it was determined that the main sewer piping under ground had channel rot and also had multiple bellies in the line. To further explain this channel rot is when the base of the piping has rotted away due to the cast iron becoming brittle and thin. A belly in the sewer line is when the pipe has dropped elevation from the original installation point.  When cast iron piping does this, the joints will break and the piping is no longer sealed which will allow the sewage to escape into the ground. If the sewer line is not repaired any trees in the area will have its roots growing into the sewer main. 
The technician has provided a new solution for the homeowner and is waiting approval.

This is to replace the main sewer from the curb to the house on the exterior of the home and from the exterior wall in the basement to the sewer stack above ground. The technician will abandon the piping under the concrete and will eliminate the floor drain and the washer drain coming from the floor.  The technician will tie onto the excising piping where each fixture meets the sewer stack.  The old piping that was in the floor will be cut flush to the floor and will be filled with concrete. On the outside of the home the technician will remove two bushes in front of the electrical meter and will install the sewer trap in that location.  The technician will install another clean out by the street per code.  

The technician will first dig down to gain access to the piping and will remove the old piping from the house to the street.  Once the old piping is removed the technician will then place stone under the piping and trap and will check for proper operation.  The sewer repair will also be inspected by a third party and after it is approved the technician will place stone over top of the piping to completely surround the pipe. The technician will then backfill the trench using the dirt that was removed and tamping as it is being installed. The technician will leave the ground at a rough grade finish and will remove any dirt and the bushes that were removed.  The homeowner will be responsible to completely surround the landscaping.

The technician will be replacing about 40’ of piping and the depth is 8’ deep. The technician would remove the ground covering plants in the mulched in area.  

The technician will first mark the area to be dug and the place the PA1 call for safe digging. The technician would then dig down exposing the piping and would make a clean cut to tie onto and then remove the old selections of cast iron piping. The technician would the place stone on the bottom of the trench and install the piping.  The technician would install a new trap at the house and then install a clean out where the current trap is. The technician would then test for proper pitch and test the sewer. The technician will also have a third party inspection completed and after passing would begin by placing stone on the top side of the pipe. The technician would then begin to back fill the trench using the soil that was removed. The technician will tamp the ground as filling to help prevent any settling and will leave the ground at a rough finish. 

The homeowner would be responsible for any landscaping.

-Let all components dry completely before reassembly

-Brushed burners with a steel brush to remove and debris in/on the face of the burners 
-Wiped top/inside of furnace with simple green and a rag

-Brushed and vacuumed secondary heat exchanger 
-Reassembled and rewired blower into bottom cabinet

-Removed burner manifold from the old gas valve 
-Cleaned pipe connections with a rag to remove any old pipe sealant in/on pipe 
-Reapplied new sealant to necessary connections
-Installed manifold onto new gas valve, screwed manifold with gas valve into place on furnace burner box 
-Reinstalled preexisting black piping onto inlet of gas valve 
-Clean all connections of excess sealant 
-Ran furnace and tested for leakage on all joints

Call Description: 
Scope of Work Includes

1. Complete Exterior Electrical Service Replacement

* Remove and replace the existing meter base with a new 200 Amp meter base.
* Replace the existing main service entrance cable with new service conductors.
* Install a new service head and associated service components as required for the existing service configuration.
* Replace the damaged underground conduit connection at the meter base and properly secure the new installation.
* Properly seal the meter base and associated entry points to help prevent future moisture intrusion.
* Install protective conduit over the exterior service cable where applicable to help protect against sunlight exposure, physical damage, and premature insulation deterioration.

2. New 200 Amp Exterior Emergency Disconnect

* Install a new 200 Amp exterior emergency service disconnect as part of the upgraded electrical service.
* Properly connect and configure the disconnect in accordance with applicable electrical codes and utility requirements.
* Install the required identification and labeling.
* Verify proper operation as part of the completed installation.

The exterior emergency disconnect provides an accessible means of shutting off electrical power to the home during an emergency or when electrical service work is required. This improves accessibility for emergency responders and electrical service personnel and brings the service configuration up to applicable requirements.

3. Interior Electrical Panel Replacement

* Remove the existing approximately 35-year-old Siemens electrical panel.
* Install a new 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel.
* Transfer and properly terminate the existing branch circuit wiring.
* Install appropriately sized breakers for the existing circuits.
* Inspect accessible conductors and connections for signs of heat damage, corrosion, or deterioration.
* Properly label the new panel and identify the branch circuits.
* Test the completed installation and verify proper operation.

4. Whole-Home Surge Protection

* Install a whole-home surge protective device at the new electrical panel.
* Properly integrate the device into the electrical system.
* Verify proper installation and operation.

Whole-home surge protection helps protect sensitive electronics, appliances, and other connected equipment against damaging voltage surges caused by lightning, utility disturbances, and other electrical events.

5. Complete Grounding and Bonding Upgrade

* Install or upgrade the grounding electrode system as required by applicable electrical codes.
* Install two grounding electrodes where required and connect them using properly sized grounding electrode conductors.
* Verify and correct the bonding of applicable metal water piping and other qualifying metal systems.
* Properly configure the grounding and bonding connections at the new service equipment.
* Verify the completed grounding and bonding system.

An effective grounding and bonding system provides an essential path for fault current and helps protective devices operate as intended during electrical faults. This upgrade is an important part of establishing a properly configured and reliable electrical service.

6. Permits, Inspections, and Utility Coordination

* Coordinate with PPL as required for the service replacement.
* Obtain the necessary permits and arrange required inspections.
* Complete the installation in accordance with applicable electrical codes and utility requirements.
* Test the completed electrical service and verify proper operation.

The technician explained that because the toilet had not been used regularly, the water in the trap had evaporated. He recommended flushing the toilet once every 2–3 weeks to maintain the water seal and prevent sewer gas odors from entering the home. When the technician attempted to flush the downstairs toilet, it failed to operate due to a severely deteriorated flapper that had completely detached from the flush handle. The homeowner initially requested that the toilet be rebuilt. During the repair process, the technician discovered that the tank-to-bowl gasket had also failed and would require replacement. After explaining the additional repairs needed, the technician recommended replacing the toilet altogether. Given that the toilet was over 30 years old and the combined cost of the necessary repairs was comparable to the cost of a new toilet, replacement was determined to be the more practical and cost-effective option. The technician replaced the existing toilet with a new comfort-height, elongated toilet. Upon completion, the toilet was tested and confirmed to be operating properly. Technician also used a toilet auger in the master bathroom to verify nothing was partially clogged in the toilet. All connections are secure, and there are currently no leaks present. Findings when on site:
Upon arrival the technician located the sewer main to the left of the driveway.  The technician then used a sewer camera to inspect the sewer main in both directions, to the house and to the street.  The technician found 2 small dents in the top of the piping going to the house and nothing going to the street. The technician did find that the whole house trap is cast iron and appears to be holding sludge in the line. Any cast iron piping underground has a life expectancy of approximately 30-40 years before it starts go bad. Replacing the cast iron trap with PVC would allow for better flow through the trap and less sludge build up. The technician will provided a solution to replace the trap with a new PVC trap.
 What the repair would look like:
The technician will mark the work to be done prior to be done for the pa1 call.  The pa1 call will mark any ground utilities prior to the excavation.  The technician will arrive on the day of the job and will begin by digging the old trap up and the dirt around the trap.  The technician will then make clean cuts on all piping to be attached to.  The technician will then place stone under the new trap and piping and will install the new trap and piping.  The new trap and piping will be checked for proper pitch and flow.  After the install there will be a third party inspection complete and approved and then additional stone will be placed around the piping. Once all stone is installed the dirt will be placed back into the trench tamped as it is installed.  The yard will then be left at a rough grade and any dirt not used in the fill process will be removed.  The homeowner would then be responsible for completing any landscaping.

We did a thorough evaluation starting at the main electrical panel and then worked our way to the troubleshoot the receptacles. We did identify a tripped GFI breaker that controls the bathroom receptacles. We showed this breaker to Martha and she confirmed that she was trying to reset the other GFI breaker that controls the exterior receptacles. Before we replaced the GFI breakers last year, the old singular GFI breaker controlled both the outside and bathroom receptacles, which is why Martha thought the whole circuit was not functioning. We were able to identify that the powder receptacle was broken, exposing one of the hot conductors which could’ve been the main culprit of why the circuit was tripped in the first place. After resetting the breaker, no immediate issues arose during today’s electrical inspection, so we determined that the broken receptacle was the main culprit. We provided options to replace both receptacles in both bathrooms, not only to fix the broken receptacle, but to also replace the second one as preventative maintenance. This option was approved, completed today, and Martha’s approved the finished work. Both receptacles were tested and working properly prior to leaving today as well. e.442908287:
Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection
LPH will install a premium whole-home surge protection device at the home’s main electrical panel. This device is designed to protect the home’s electrical system and connected equipment from damaging voltage spikes and transient surges before they can travel throughout the home’s wiring.
Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but the majority of power surges actually originate inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and even garage door openers create small electrical surges—known as microsurges—every time their motors cycle on and off. While each individual surge is small, thousands of these microsurges occur over time and gradually wear down the sensitive electronic components found in today’s modern appliances and equipment.
Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these surges away from the home’s electrical system, reducing cumulative damage to expensive electronics and appliances. This is especially important in newer homes, where nearly every major appliance contains sophisticated circuit boards and microprocessors that are far more sensitive to voltage fluctuations than older equipment.
In addition to protecting against internally generated microsurges, whole-home surge protection also provides a critical first line of defense against larger surges originating from the utility company, switching events on the electrical grid, nearby lightning strikes, or power being restored after an outage.
Benefits of premium whole-home surge protection include:
	• Protects HVAC systems, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
	• Helps safeguard sensitive electronics such as televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart home devices.
	• Reduces the long-term effects of everyday microsurges that slowly degrade electronic components.
	• Can help extend the service life of modern appliances and equipment by reducing electrical stress on internal circuit boards.
	• Helps minimize the likelihood of costly repairs or premature equipment replacement due to surge damage.
	• Provides continuous protection for the entire home’s electrical system without relying solely on individual plug-in surge strips.
	• Offers added peace of mind during storms, utility switching events, and unexpected power outages.
As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

Premium Surge Protection Warranty & Replacement Coverage

The installed surge protection device also provides additional protection beyond the device itself. If the surge protector is ever sacrificed or fails as a result of a covered surge event, the device is backed by a lifetime warranty and coverage of up to $100,000 toward covered damage to the home’s electrical components and connected equipment, subject to the manufacturer’s warranty terms and conditions.

If the surge protector ever needs to be replaced under the warranty, the replacement device is provided at no charge. LPH will also handle the replacement installation for a $150 labor charge, helping make future warranty replacement straightforward and affordable for the homeowner.

This means the homeowner is not simply purchasing a surge protector—they are adding a long-term layer of protection to the home’s electrical system while also having manufacturer-backed coverage in the event of a significant surge.

As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

	• Protects HVAC systems, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
	• Helps safeguard sensitive electronics such as televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart home devices.
	• Reduces the long-term effects of everyday microsurges that slowly degrade electronic components.
	• Can help extend the service life of modern appliances and equipment by reducing electrical stress on internal circuit boards.
	• Helps minimize the likelihood of costly repairs or premature equipment replacement due to surge damage.
	• Provides continuous protection for the entire home’s electrical system without relying solely on individual plug-in surge strips.
	• Offers added peace of mind during storms, utility switching events, and unexpected power outages.
As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

Premium Surge Protection Warranty & Replacement Coverage

The installed surge protection device also provides additional protection beyond the device itself. If the surge protector is ever sacrificed or fails as a result of a covered surge event, the device is backed by a lifetime warranty and coverage of up to $100,000 toward covered damage to the home’s electrical components and connected equipment, subject to the manufacturer’s warranty terms and conditions.

If the surge protector ever needs to be replaced under the warranty, the replacement device is provided at no charge. LPH will also handle the replacement installation for a $150 labor charge, helping make future warranty replacement straightforward and affordable for the homeowner.

This means the homeowner is not simply purchasing a surge protector—they are adding a long-term layer of protection to the home’s electrical system while also having manufacturer-backed coverage in the event of a significant surge.

As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

LPH was dispatched today due to the homeowner expressing concerns regarding the outdoor unit. The homeowner reported that the indoor air handler was operating and blowing air; however, the outdoor unit was making a vibrating or humming noise while the outdoor heat pump fan was not running.

Upon arrival, LPH found the system was operating at that time. LPH performed a full system diagnostic but was unable to recreate the condition described by the homeowner. LPH manually initiated defrost mode multiple times and verified that the system was functioning properly throughout each cycle.

LPH explained to the homeowner that the condition she observed was most likely the heat pump entering its normal defrost cycle due to the low outdoor temperature. The outdoor temperature that morning was approximately 25°F. During the diagnostic, LPH also noticed that the outdoor unit was slightly low on refrigerant.

LPH added a small amount of refrigerant to bring the system back to proper operating conditions. A leak search was performed on both the indoor and outdoor units. No active refrigerant leaks were detected. However, LPH did notice oil residue around the liquid line flare nut connection near the service port. LPH also found that all service port caps were loose.

LPH tightened all service port caps and secured the liquid line connection. The liquid line nut was able to be tightened further, indicating that the connection may have been allowing refrigerant to escape. Once tightened, no further signs of leakage were detected.

After completing the repairs and adjustments, LPH verified proper system operation. The system is currently operating as intended, and no additional issues were observed at the time of departure.

This process uses significantly less electricity while still providing the same amount of hot water.

	•	Hybrid Mode – Automatically balances heat pump and electric elements for efficiency and performance
	•	Electric Mode – Operates like a standard electric water heater when high demand is needed
	•	Energy Saver Mode – Optimizes performance for reduced energy consumption

Because the unit utilizes ambient air to assist in heating the water, it can reduce energy usage by up to 60–70% compared to a standard electric water heater, which can lead to significant savings on utility bills over time.

Hybrid water heaters also typically qualify for energy efficiency rebates and potential tax incentives, making them a cost-effective long-term investment.

i.442935720: We were called out to evaluate why Clair’s whole home standby generator was giving him an overcrank fault and not turning on at all. Upon arrival, we spoke with Clair, who informed us that he wanted to test his whole home generator to make sure it functions in the event of a power loss due to today’s severe weather. When testing, he noticed that his app notified him of the error code E1100(overcrank fault) and the unit would not turn on. We attempted to diagnosis this issue over the phone, but was unsuccessful which prompted our in person arrival. Upon diagnostic of this unit, we did a manual error code reset by, holding the off button until the blinking light disappeared on the side of the unit. We then waited a few minutes before doing a manual startup which prompted the motor to attempt to run for a few seconds and then it kicked on. We then let this motor run for about 5 to 10 minutes to make sure the oil, fuel, and air properly cycled through to prevent any internal damage. After this was completed, we then turned the unit back to auto mode. This unit then automatically idled down for standby mode, prior to our departure today. Upon speaking with Clair, he informed us that he does not remember this unit doing any weekly or daily test since the installation. If that’s the case, then our assumption for the over cranking issue was due to too much oxygen inside the fuel lines from sitting stagnant for so long. We informed Clair that if he has any other issues with his app or the generator itself, to contact us or the Generac support team as soon as possible. We thank you for trusting LPH for your electrical concern and we look forward to servicing in the future. We hope you have a happy Thanksgiving and happy holidays for the remainder of this year!
